work.title: DEBATE ROOM
work.subtitle: 论证练习课
work.scope: Fictional adult learning exercises. Illustrations are not records of real participants or research evidence. No accredited qualification or actual learner outcomes are supplied.

pages.title: Set a bounded discussion question.
pages.lead: This course practises building and examining arguments. The issue is fictional: should an imagined reading group use one shared text or offer several choices?
pages.body: The aim is to make reasoning visible, not to declare a universally correct policy or evaluate a real group. Keep the discussion within the stated exercise.
pages.subheading: Issue / scope / decision not being made
pages.detail: Working record: Write the discussion question and one real-world conclusion it cannot settle. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write the discussion question and one real-world conclusion it cannot settle.

pages.title: Agree on the important terms.
pages.lead: Arguments become difficult to compare when speakers use the same word in different ways. Define the terms needed for this discussion before collecting reasons.
pages.body: Shared text could mean one extract for one meeting, not a permanent reading rule. Choice could refer to selecting among three extracts rather than unrestricted material.
pages.detail: Working record: Define shared, choice and useful for this particular exercise. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Define shared, choice and useful for this particular exercise.

pages.title: Map a claim to its reasons.
pages.lead: State a claim, the reason offered for it and the assumption connecting them. A reason is not yet evidence, and the connecting assumption may be disputed.
pages.body: Claim: one extract could focus the conversation. Reason: everyone can refer to the same passage. Assumption: a common reference is helpful for the intended discussion.
pages.detail: Working record: Build a three-part argument without claiming an observed learning outcome. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Build a three-part argument without claiming an observed learning outcome.

pages.title: Support the first position.
pages.lead: Develop the strongest bounded version of the shared-text argument. Separate a plausible mechanism from information that would be needed to establish it in practice.
pages.body: A common passage may make references easier to locate. Whether that actually helps a particular group remains a question requiring suitable observation and participant context.
pages.detail: Working record: Write one strong supporting reason and the source needed to test its relevance. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write one strong supporting reason and the source needed to test its relevance.

pages.title: Represent the alternative fairly.
pages.lead: Build a version of the multiple-choice argument that its supporter would recognise. Do not weaken it simply to make your preferred position easier to defend.
pages.body: Choice might let readers connect discussion to their interests. It could also make references harder to share. Both points belong in an honest comparison.
pages.subheading: Alternative claim / strongest reason / acknowledged cost
pages.detail: Working record: Write the alternative argument before adding your response. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write the alternative argument before adding your response.

pages.title: Evaluate a source before using it.
pages.lead: Ask whether a source addresses the actual question, how it was produced and what it cannot establish. This exercise supplies no real empirical study.
pages.body: A fictional preference quote can illustrate a viewpoint but cannot establish what most readers prefer. A beautiful illustration is not evidence about reading outcomes.
pages.subheading: Source type / relevance / limit / permitted use
pages.detail: Working record: Classify an invented quotation and explain the narrow use you would allow. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Classify an invented quotation and explain the narrow use you would allow.

pages.title: Ask a question that could matter.
pages.lead: A useful challenge targets an assumption or a missing link rather than the speaker’s character. Give the other person room to clarify the argument.
pages.body: Question: does the benefit of a common reference depend on the kind of discussion? That asks for a condition rather than assuming that the original claim is foolish.
pages.subheading: Target claim / questioned assumption / clarification request
pages.detail: Working record: Write two respectful challenges addressed to different parts of the argument. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write two respectful challenges addressed to different parts of the argument.

pages.title: Respond without changing the subject.
pages.lead: A response should identify the challenge, answer the part you can address and acknowledge what remains unresolved. It is acceptable to narrow the original claim.
pages.body: A revised response might say a shared extract could help a close-reading exercise, while a broader discussion might benefit from several choices. The claim is now more conditional.
pages.detail: Working record: Answer one question and add a qualification that genuinely changes the claim. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Answer one question and add a qualification that genuinely changes the claim.

pages.title: Revise the argument map.
pages.lead: Update the claim, reasons and assumptions together. If the claim becomes narrower, check that the supporting reasons still address the revised version.
pages.body: Replace one text is best with one shared extract may suit a session focused on close comparison. The revision concerns task fit rather than a universal ranking.
pages.subheading: Earlier claim / revised claim / retained reason / removed assumption
pages.detail: Working record: Revise the map and cross out a reason that no longer fits. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Revise the map and cross out a reason that no longer fits.

pages.title: State a provisional position.
pages.lead: Finish with the position you can currently support, its strongest reason and a condition that could change your view. A provisional position is not a failure to decide.
pages.body: For this invented close-reading session, a shared extract is a defensible starting option. Information about the actual group, purpose and materials could change that choice.
pages.detail: Working record: Write a closing position that leaves its evidence boundary visible. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write a closing position that leaves its evidence boundary visible.
